technique: withholding — what the poem refuses to name or explain, and why that works
lesson:
Today we work on one tool: withholding. That means the poem leaves something out on purpose, so you lean in to supply it.

Watch the woman. The poem says "think of her," then "the ache she's carrying," then "a little under the weather." It never tells you who she is to him. Wife, mother, sister, friend—the poem refuses to say. It also never names what the ache is.

It works because your mind wants to fill a gap. When the poem skips a fact, you reach for it yourself. You guess at her. That guessing makes her matter more to you than a full explanation would, because you did the work.

Try this: write about a person, but cut the line that says who they are and what's wrong. Leave only what the speaker does.

The second time through, hold onto how little you're actually told about her, and feel yourself filling it in anyway.

Here is the poem.
poem:
The kettle starts its small complaint, and you
let it, because the knife has found the bread
and that comes first—the heel end, going dry,
sawed thin and laid to brown in the black pan
where yesterday's fat still remembers heat.
You butter it standing up, no plate, the way
a man eats who's got somewhere to be by four.
Last night the sky was scrubbed clean to the bone—
the seven sisters up over the ridge in their cold
huddle, bright as struck flint, the way they've hung
this same dark week for every soul who ever
banked a fire in these hills and rose to cold.
The bread's done. You turn it once and think of her,
the ache she's carrying, small and real as weather—

Someone who's a little under the weather is counting the hours till you turn up—pull on your boots and be the good part of her day.
